Cycloids

CurvesAlgebraArea
Game: A wheel rolls along, and pencils fixed to it draw curious curves; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Press the picture to fix a pencil to the wheel (or use the Add buttons), then press Start and watch what each one draws. Try the rolling-inside and rolling-outside wheels too.

Press the picture to add a mark. Space or Enter starts and stops; the right arrow steps ahead.

Wheel
Roll / rotate 1 R / r –
Look for the math

Roll a coin along a table, with a dot painted on its edge. The path the dot follows is a cycloid. Here you can put the dot anywhere on the wheel, or roll the wheel round a circle instead.

The ordinary cycloid

A dot on the rim touches the line once every time the wheel has rolled its own circumference, 2πr, and each arch is exactly 8r long and encloses 3πr², three times the wheel's own area. The logic test measured both by walking along the curve in small steps. A dot inside the wheel makes a gentler wave without points (a curtate cycloid); a dot outside it, such as on a flange, loops back on itself (a prolate cycloid).

Rolling round a circle

Roll the wheel inside a fixed circle and a rim dot draws a hypocycloid; roll it outside and it draws an epicycloid. When the ratio R/r of the circle's radius to the wheel's is a whole number k, either curve has exactly k sharp points (cusps) and closes after one trip round. With R/r = 2 inside, the dot moves along a straight line (the Tusi couple); with 3 it is a deltoid; with 4 it is the astroid, x2/3 + y2/3 = R2/3, which the test checked point by point. Outside with R/r = 1 it is the cardioid, of length 16r and area 6πr².

Roll / rotate

The Roll / rotate number says how fast the wheel spins compared with rolling without slipping: 1 is true rolling, 2 twice as fast, 1/2 half as fast, 0 no spin at all. Rolling round a circle, a wheel that rolls truly spins R/r + 1 times for every trip round outside, and R/r − 1 times, the other way, inside. The page gives each position in two ways, by formula and by turning the dots a little each step, and the test found the two agree.

The page this puzzle is linked to is a reader’s question about cycloids and does not contain the applet; the rules here come from the applet itself. The applet cut the radius R/r down to whole pixels, so some of its curves do not quite close; this port uses the exact value.

Add three marks (inside, on the rim, outside) on a wheel rolling on a line and press Start. Then try rolling inside a circle with R/r = 4.
